subject: Applied Mathematics
title: V. Fourier Series and Partial Differential Equations

segments.text: This chapter extends the toolkit from Chapter IV in two connected directions: representing periodic functions as sums of simple sine and cosine waves (Fourier series), and solving equations involving functions of more than one variable (partial differential equations, or PDEs) — together, these are the standard tools for analysing systems that vary in both space and time, such as heat flow or vibrating strings.

blocks.text: 3. Formation and classification of basic PDEs

blocks.text: 5. Standard heat, wave, and Laplace equations

Solving each with given boundary conditions (via separation of variables) typically produces a solution as an infinite Fourier series — directly connecting the two halves of this chapter: the separation-of-variables solution’s spatial part is expanded in a Fourier series to match the specific initial or boundary shape of the problem.

items.text: Fourier series decompose periodic functions into sine/cosine components, with coefficients isolated via the orthogonality of sines and cosines over one period.
Even/odd symmetry immediately determines whether a Fourier series needs only cosine or only sine terms, substantially simplifying calculation.
PDEs are classified as elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic, mirroring conic section classification and predicting the equation’s qualitative behaviour and appropriate conditions.

Separation of variables converts a PDE into a pair of ODEs by introducing a separation constant, exploiting the fact that expressions depending on different independent variables can only be equal if both equal the same constant.
The heat, wave, and Laplace equations are the three canonical PDEs of applied mathematics, and their solutions with realistic boundary conditions typically emerge as Fourier series.
